name: Zopiclone

lead: Zopiclone is a prescription sleeping pill used in Europe, Canada and elsewhere for short-term severe insomnia. People interested in looks tie deeper sleep to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling at the benzodiazepine site, causing sedation. Marketed since 1986, it has been studied for insomnia; appearance has not been studied. It is not approved in the US, where its (S)-enantiomer eszopiclone is used. Some forum posters say sleeping pills lower sleep quality over time.

paras: It is taken at bedtime on prescription, with treatment usually limited to about four weeks. Users describe it as a short-term bridge during bad stretches of sleep rather than a long-term routine.
Reported effects include drowsiness, a bitter taste, amnesia, behavioural changes, tolerance and dependence. It is not approved in the US, and treatment is usually kept to about four weeks.

angle.text: Zopiclone is a prescription Z-drug sleeping pill used for severe insomnia outside the US. The idea is deeper sleep, better recovery, then clearer skin and a more rested face. Some forum posters say sleeping pills lower sleep quality over time.

lead: Zopiclone is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class (a 'Z-drug') used for short-term treatment of severe insomnia in adults. It acts at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. [1][2]

It has no appearance indication. Its link to looks is indirect and runs through sleep: people who take it are trying to fall asleep, and sleep is a topic that appearance-focused communities discuss alongside skin, recovery and training. On looksmax.org it appears in occasional threads about sleep aids and long-term use. [3]

Zopiclone was developed by Rhone-Poulenc (now part of Sanofi) and introduced in 1986 under names such as Imovane and Zimovane. It is not approved in the United States, where its (S)-enantiomer eszopiclone (Lunesta) is sold, but it is a prescription medicine in the UK, Canada, Australia, much of Europe and elsewhere. [1][2]
infobox: About 5 hours; about 7 to 9 hours in people aged 65 and over [2]
About 75 to 80 percent, peak at 1 to 2 hours [2]
Liver, mainly CYP3A4 and CYP2E1; about 80 percent excreted in urine [2]
Prescription-only; UK Class C, US Schedule IV since 2005 (marketed in the US only as eszopiclone) [2]

paras: Zopiclone is indicated for short-term treatment of severe insomnia causing distress or functional impairment. The NHS says it is usually prescribed for a few days to a few weeks and generally not for more than four weeks, because the body can become tolerant and the drug may work less well. [4] A 2023 European guideline advises against use beyond four weeks. [2][5]

According to Wikipedia, drugs in this group shorten the time to fall asleep by about 10 to 20 minutes but have not been shown to clearly increase total sleep time. [2][5] Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is described there as superior to zopiclone, with benefits lasting at least a year. [2]

Researchers have also tested it for other sleep-related purposes: a registered phase 3 trial of 264 people studied whether zopiclone changed compliance with continuous positive airway pressure treatment in obstructive sleep apnea, and a small trial in central sleep apnea with heart failure was terminated after enrolling two people. [6][7]

Zopiclone enhances GABA-A receptor signalling at the benzodiazepine binding site, producing sedative, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects. [2] A review of insomnia drugs beyond benzodiazepines covers the pharmacology of the Z-drugs alongside other classes of insomnia treatment. [8] Wikipedia notes that in the racemic mixture the dextrorotatory enantiomer has higher exposure than the levorotatory one, and eszopiclone is the single-enantiomer product. [2]

Oral bioavailability is about 75 to 80 percent, with peak levels at 1 to 2 hours and protein binding around 52 to 59 percent. The half-life is about 5 hours and longer in older adults. The liver metabolises it mainly through CYP3A4 and CYP2E1, so drugs that inhibit or induce those enzymes, such as erythromycin, itraconazole and rifampicin, change its levels. In liver disease it clears much more slowly. [2]

EEG studies summarised on Wikipedia show that zopiclone reduces slow-wave sleep and total REM sleep, delays REM onset and increases stage 2 sleep and beta activity, effects that resemble those of benzodiazepines, with rebound disturbances of sleep architecture on withdrawal. [2] This is the background to forum comments that sleeping pills change sleep quality. [3]

The NHS lists dry mouth, a bitter or metallic taste, and tiredness, sleepiness or reduced alertness the next day. [4] The British National Formulary, as summarised by Wikipedia, adds nausea, dizziness and headache. [2]

Rarer effects include amnesia, confusion, depression, hallucinations, nightmares and sleepwalking or other activity while not fully awake. [2][4] Wikipedia notes associations between sleeping pills and higher mortality risk, and in older adults with poorer balance, falls and hip fractures. [2] A 2005 BMJ meta-analysis examined risks and benefits of sedative hypnotics, including zopiclone, in older people with insomnia. [9]

Tolerance can develop within days to weeks, and the drug carries a dependence liability. Stopping abruptly can cause agitation, anxiety and rebound insomnia, so clinicians usually reduce the amount gradually. [2][4] A review of case reports and epidemiological data examined abuse and dependence potential for zolpidem and zopiclone. [10] Wikipedia notes that animal studies found monkeys would self-administer it. [2]

The NHS advises avoiding driving, cycling or machinery for 12 hours after a dose and says alcohol increases the effects, including breathing problems. [4] Wikipedia cites estimates of roughly a 50 percent increase in accident risk and a military-oriented study in which zopiclone's impairment lasted longer than zaleplon's or temazepam's. [2] A 1998 Lancet study examined road-traffic accidents and benzodiazepine use. [11]

Other sedatives, opioids, antipsychotics, antidepressants, epilepsy medicines and sedating antihistamines may interact. [4] Combining zopiclone with alcohol, opioids or other central nervous system depressants raises the risk of excessive sedation and breathing problems. [2]
The NHS says zopiclone is not usually used in pregnancy but may be prescribed briefly if sleep problems are severe and other treatments have failed. It passes into breast milk in small amounts. [4]

A randomised trial compared cognitive behavioural therapy with zopiclone for chronic insomnia in older adults. [12] A BMJ meta-analysis examined short-term sedative hypnotics including zopiclone in older people. [9] A comparative meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy and behaviour therapy for persistent insomnia is also in the literature. [13] A Lancet network meta-analysis covers hypnotics for insomnia. [14] A registered phase 3 non-inferiority trial of 263 people compared eszopiclone with zopiclone. [15] Wikipedia notes a 2004 meta-analysis finding few clear differences between zopiclone and benzodiazepines on most outcomes. [2] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

Zopiclone was developed by Rhone-Poulenc and introduced in 1986, initially promoted as an improvement on benzodiazepines, a claim Wikipedia says was later found not to hold. [2] Grokipedia reports a first patent in 1972. [1] Wikipedia's article on Z-drugs states that zopiclone was approved in the UK by 1989, followed by zolpidem; zaleplon was approved in the US in 1999 and eszopiclone in 2005. [5] Sepracor began marketing eszopiclone in the US in 2005, and on 4 April 2005 the US DEA placed zopiclone in Schedule IV. [2]
Wikipedia lists zopiclone as prescription-only in Australia (Schedule 4) and Canada, Class C in the UK, Schedule IV in the US, Class B1 in Brazil and Class C5 (restricted) in New Zealand. [2]

Wikipedia reports that zopiclone is sometimes misused, often with alcohol, that the Canadian Compendium of Pharmaceuticals and Specialties recommends prescriptions not exceed 7 to 10 days, that it is frequently found in suspected drugged-driving cases, and that it is among the top ten medicines obtained with false prescriptions in France. [2] On T Nation, a 2010 thread about opiate withdrawal mentions a family member withdrawing from oxycodone and Imovane that had been taken without a prescription. [16]

Zopiclone appears only occasionally in appearance forums. In one looksmax.org thread a user who said poor sleep had long been a problem asked whether others had taken it long-term and noticed side effects; replies said dependence is the side effect and that all sleep drugs interfere with REM sleep and sleep cycles. [3]
